summary: I checked the data handling, grouping, replicate averaging and the claims in DATA_LEAKAGE_AUDIT.md against the code (src/data/datasets.py, src/training/learning_curves.py, src/evaluation/forecast_experiment.py, experiments/refinement.py, experiments/analysis.py, experiments/robustness.py) and the raw OSSL, mango, Eigenvector and Tecator files. Several controls work as claimed. Replicate scans are averaged (I recounted 5,111 duplicate KSSL-VisNIR layer scans). Neospectra is restricted to the 2,106 multi-scanner averages. Pre-processing is sample-wise. The eigen-spectrum comes from the pool only, and forecasters receive only pilot data. Five problems remain, and some change stated conclusions. (1) For 12 of the 38 tasks (all ICRAF and Neospectra tasks), layers without coordinates are put in singleton groups even though their profile or site can be recovered. As a result, 9–12% of each of these test sets shares a profile with the pool, which contradicts 'every split is group-disjoint'. (2) 2,084 of the 2,106 Neospectra soils are KSSL archive layers, and 96–100% of their reference values are identical to the KSSL values. The leave-one-source-out (LOSO) transfer still treats Neospectra and KSSL as independent sources. When the two are merged, SLOPE-T's advantage over RPM and FLAT disappears (mean error 0.251 → 0.262; vs RPM raw p = 0.18). (3) The 38 tasks are heavily pseudo-replicated, because the same spectra and labels are reused across libraries and properties. At the level of the 9 sources, the RPM-w > RPM result disappears and the significance levels shrink by orders of magnitude. (4) For the small data sets (Tecator, Diesel, Tablets, CGL), the 'ground truth' comes from one test split of 58–164 samples and is dominated by a few outlying samples (bootstrap SE of the test log-RMSE 0.09–0.26). (5) The claim of nominal coverage for calibrated bands is a pooled average dominated by soil forecasts; for the non-soil sources, coverage of the 80% bands is 29–76%. Most fixes are re-analyses of existing outputs. Correcting the soil groups and the small-set ground truth needs targeted reruns.
strengths: Replicate handling is largely correct and verifiable. I recounted 29,082 KSSL-VisNIR scans covering 23,971 layers (5,111 extra scans, as stated in the audit), which are averaged per layer before splitting (datasets.py L81). Neospectra is correctly restricted to the 2,106 'Multiple' (multi-scanner-averaged) rows. The mango fruit reconstruction is sound: 3,617 of 4,021 reconstructed fruits have two scans, the within-pair SNV-RMS distance (median 0.0020) is far smaller than the between-fruit distance (median 0.263), and the 404 single-scan 'fruits' have no near-identical spectral neighbour in the same lot (only 10 of 404 lie closer than 0.005).

Unlabelled spectra and penalty grids for the main forecasters come from the pool only (forecast_experiment.py L63–64; run_truth L39). Forecasters receive only (X0, y0, g0). Pre-processing is strictly row-wise, and this is unit-tested (test_snv_rowwise_only).

All transferred quantities (r prior, SLOPE-T slope, conformal quantiles) were designed as leave-one-source-out. Per-pilot raw results, truth curves and pool/test indices are saved, which made the re-analyses in this review possible.
The time-stamped experiment log and the pre-registration openly separate pre-registered from post-hoc elements.

issues.title: Soil profile/site groups are incomplete for all ICRAF and Neospectra tasks: 9–12% of each test set shares a profile or site with the pool
issues.description: The ICRAF-ISRIC site file has no site-ID column, and Neospectra has none either, so load_ossl falls back to rounded coordinates. Layers without coordinates get a singleton group 'L_<layer id>' (datasets.py L102–110). For ICRAF-ISRIC, 438 of 4,073 layers (10.8%) have no coordinates. These layers form whole profiles with consecutive sample numbers and layer sequence 1..k; for example, FS15R_FS4268–FS4274 is one 7-layer Brazilian profile. Each such layer becomes its own group. For Neospectra, 16% of layers lack coordinates, but every averaged spectrum carries id.kssl.lay_local_txt, which maps to the KSSL site ID. This identifier was available but not used. Because both the test split and every LOGO/grouped CV in pilots and truth fits rely on these labels, sibling layers of one profile are split between test and pool, and are treated as independent inside pilots. This contradicts Section 3.2 ('Soil layers from the same site or profile were assigned to the same group. Every split is group-disjoint') and the 'without data leakage' contribution (Introduction, contribution iii). The audit's verification (test_split_is_group_disjoint_and_complete) uses synthetic labels. It can only show that a split respects the labels it is given, not that those labels match real profiles.
issues.evidence: Recomputed with the project's own loader and the saved truth_*.npz pool/test indices (scripts in /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R5/grp_leak*.py and leak_effect.py). ICRAF: I reconstructed profiles from consecutive IDs and layer sequence; the reconstruction agrees with the coordinate groups for 98.5% of profiles that have coordinates. This gives 72–82 coordinate-less profiles (median 5 layers). Test layers whose profile siblings are in the pool: ICRAF-VisNIR OC/clay/pH/CEC 115/926, 110/937, 111/948, 107/919 (11.6–12.4%); ICRAF-MIR 106/924, 86/936, 112/947, 92/914 (9.2–11.8%). Neospectra: grouping by the KSSL site ID (100% consistent with the coordinate groups where coordinates exist), 50/527, 54/526, 46/525, 60/524 test layers (8.8–11.5%) share a site with the pool. Effect: ridge at the LOGO-selected penalty, trained on the full pool, gives a lower MSE on these leaked layers when their siblings are in the pool than when the siblings are removed. ICRAF-VisNIR:OC 0.077 vs 0.096 (−20%); ICRAF-VisNIR:clay −11%; ICRAF-MIR:OC −3%; Neospectra:OC 0.051 vs 0.068 (−24%); Neospectra:clay −12%. Errors on non-leaked layers are unchanged. On the whole test set this shifts the log-RMSE by −0.005 to −0.012 at the full pool size. The bias is therefore small, but real and largest at the largest n.
issues.corrective_action: Rebuild the groups. For ICRAF-ISRIC, use the ISRIC profile code, or reconstruct profiles from sample-number runs and layer sequence. For Neospectra, map id.kssl.lay_local_txt to the KSSL id.dataset.site_ascii_txt. Never fall back to per-layer singletons without reporting it. Rerun the truth curves and pilots for the 12 affected tasks. Add a real-data assertion to the test suite that no reconstructed profile or site appears on both sides of a split. Report in the paper how many layers needed a fallback group, and correct Section 3.2 and Limitation 5.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run run_truth and run_pilots (and the refinement and ablation stages) for the 8 ICRAF and 4 Neospectra tasks with corrected groups, then recompute Tables 2–3 and S15. The compute cost is small (N ≤ 3,800 per task).

issues.title: Neospectra is a subset of KSSL but is treated as an independent 'source' in all LOSO transfers; merging them removes SLOPE-T's reported advantage
issues.description: source_of() in experiments/refinement.py L23–28 and analysis.py L48–53 defines KSSL and Neospectra as separate sources. This definition is used for the RPM-T alignment prior, the SLOPE-T slope prior (add_slope_transfer) and the LOSO split-conformal bands. The Neospectra soils, however, are KSSL archive samples analysed by the same laboratory, and 542–696 of them are physically present in the capped KSSL task sets. So the 'other sources' used to calibrate the Neospectra tasks include the same soils and the same reference values, and vice versa. The claims that SLOPE-T 'was the most accurate method overall' and was 'significantly better than the pre-registered RPM (Holm p = 0.031)' (Section 4.3, Table 2), and the practical recommendation (ii), depend on this.
issues.evidence: 2,084 of 2,106 Neospectra averaged spectra have id.kssl.lay_local_txt present in the KSSL site file. Reference values are identical to KSSL for 96.4% (OC), 96.2% (clay), 100% (pH) and 97.3% (CEC) of matched samples (overlap.py). I recomputed SLOPE-T exactly as in add_slope_transfer (my reproduction gives the reported 0.2509) but with KSSL and Neospectra merged into one source (merged2.py). Mean task error rises from 0.251 to 0.262 (KSSL tasks 0.251 → 0.288; Neospectra tasks 0.190 → 0.220). Against RPM, SLOPE-T is better on 21 of 38 tasks (reported: 25 of 38), with uncorrected Wilcoxon p = 0.18 (reported Holm p = 0.031). Against FLAT it is better on 19 of 38 tasks, 0.262 vs 0.266, p = 0.67. The 80/95% coverage of the merged-source LOSO-conformal bands for SLOPE-T is 77.0/94.1% (Table S20 reports 79.3/94.3). SLOPE-T is also highly sensitive to the transferred constant: changing the KSSL prior through the median of 30 vs 26 other tasks moves the KSSL task error by 0.037.
issues.corrective_action: Define sources by sample provenance and laboratory, not by instrument library. At minimum, merge KSSL and Neospectra, and document that ICRAF VisNIR and MIR are already merged. Recompute RPM-T priors, SLOPE-T, the conformal bands, the gain analysis (T14) and all associated statistics. Revise the claims that SLOPE-T is the most accurate method and significantly better than RPM, and soften recommendation (ii) and the abstract accordingly. Report the sensitivity of SLOPE-T to the choice of slope prior (e.g., a jackknife over sources).

issues.title: Pseudo-replication: the 38 'tasks' share spectra and reference values, so task-level Wilcoxon tests overstate the evidence
issues.description: The unit of analysis is the task (Section 3.7), but tasks are far from independent. Four properties per library are computed on the same spectra. ICRAF-MIR and ICRAF-VisNIR are the same soils with the same labels. KSSL MIR and VisNIR share most layers. Neospectra is nested in KSSL (issue 02). Six diesel properties come from essentially the same 395 spectra, and three Tecator and four CGL properties each share one spectral matrix. The effective sample size is therefore about 8–11 sources or libraries, not 38, and p-values such as 'p < 0.0001' and the 'Holm p = 0.023' for RPM-w vs RPM are not supported.
issues.evidence: Layer-ID overlap from the cached spectra: ICRAF-MIR 4,153 of 4,153 layers are also in ICRAF-VisNIR; KSSL-MIR and KSSL-VisNIR share 20,969 layers. I re-tested on per-task means from raw_results.csv after averaging within units (srcstats.py). At the 11-library level: RPM vs IPL3 better on 11 of 11, p = 0.0010; RPM vs FLAT p = 0.083; RPM vs SLOPE-T p = 0.024; RPM-w vs RPM p = 0.41 (RPM-w better on only 7 of 11). At the 9-source level: RPM vs IPL3 p = 0.0039 (the smallest p-value possible with 9 units); RPM-w vs RPM p = 0.65. With 8 sources (KSSL and Neospectra merged): RPM vs IPL3 p = 0.0078; RPM vs SLOPE-T p = 0.078. The main conclusion (RPM is better than IPL3) survives. The RPM-w refinement claim and the precision of all reported p-values do not.
issues.corrective_action: Use a hierarchical analysis: a mixed model with random effects for source, library and property, or a source-level paired test or permutation, as the primary inference. Report the effective number of independent units. Downgrade the RPM-w vs RPM statement (Section 4.3) and report source-level effect sizes alongside the task-level ones.

issues.title: The ground truth for the small data sets comes from a single test split of 58–164 samples, is dominated by a few outlying samples, and in one task even rises with n
issues.description: For Tecator (n_test = 60), CGL (58), Diesel (99) and Tablets (164), the 'true' learning curve is the expected error over training draws but on one fixed test set (split_task, test_frac 0.25). Its test-set sampling error is not reflected anywhere. No outlier screening is documented. Tecator contains the 25 samples that the data provider designated for extrapolation tests (E1/E2, the last 25 rows), and they are mixed at random into the pool and test set. Diesel:total has a truth curve that increases with n (RMSE 2.20 → 2.77 → 2.78 at n = 50, 100, 200; slope +0.117 per doubling; Monte-Carlo SE of the log truth 0.10–0.13), which signals heavy-tailed labels or outliers rather than a learning curve. These 14–15 tasks make up about 40% of the task-level statistics.
issues.evidence: I bootstrapped the test residuals of the full-pool ridge (LOGO-selected penalty from path_full) (testnoise.py). SE of the test log-RMSE: Tecator:fat 0.239, Tecator:protein 0.258, Diesel:bp50 0.224, Tablets:assay 0.171, CGL:glucose 0.121, Diesel:total 0.091. The share of test SSE from the 3 largest residuals is 61%, 70%, 55%, 53%, 37% and 27% respectively. One Tecator test sample (row 43) contributes a squared residual of 147 for fat. The largest Tablets residuals are rows 125, 126 and 18, i.e. calibration-set tablets 126, 127 and 19 of the IDRC-2002 set; the authors should check them against the outliers reported for that shoot-out. Tecator E1/E2 rows: 10 in the test set, 15 in the pool. These SEs are comparable to the mean forecast errors (0.25–0.28) and an order of magnitude larger than the between-method differences that are claimed (e.g., SLOPE-T vs FLAT 0.015). The truth arrays (truth_Diesel__total.npz: ridge_se/(2·mse) = 0.10–0.13) confirm that the truth is unstable.
issues.corrective_action: For tasks with N < 1,000, average the truth over repeated group-disjoint outer splits (e.g., 10–20), and report and propagate the uncertainty of the truth. Specify an outlier policy a priori: for Tecator, either exclude the E1/E2 extrapolation samples or analyse them separately; for Tablets, check against the known shoot-out outliers. Also report robust metrics. Flag or exclude Diesel:total, or explain why its curve rises. Report the main comparisons with and without these small sets.
issues.proposed_experiment: Repeat run_truth and run_pilots for the 15 small tasks (Diesel ×6, Tecator ×3, CGL ×4, Tablets, plus mango as a control) with 10 outer group-disjoint test splits, and evaluate forecasts against the split-averaged truth. Rerun Table 2 with and without Tecator E1/E2 and the Tablets outliers. This takes minutes of CPU time.

issues.title: The 'nominal coverage' of the cross-data-set calibrated bands is a pooled average dominated by soil forecasts; coverage fails badly for non-soil sources
issues.description: The LOSO split-conformal coverage (analysis.py L384–403; Table S20; Abstract: 'Bands calibrated across data sets reached nominal coverage'; recommendation iii) is pooled over individual forecasts. KSSL and ICRAF contribute two thirds of all forecasts because their truth grids reach n = 6,400 and 1,600. Coverage is therefore driven by soil libraries, while the fuel, pharmaceutical and mixture sets, where users would need the bands most, are severely under-covered. This is a distribution bias of the task collection (23 of 38 tasks are OSSL soils) carried directly into a headline claim.
issues.evidence: I recomputed the T16 procedure per source for the 80% bands (confsrc.py). Pooled SLOPE-T coverage is 79.2%, matching the reported 79.3%. SLOPE-T 80% coverage per source: CGL 28.7%, Tablets 37.5%, Diesel 49.6%, Tecator 76.1%, AfSIS1 80.6%, KSSL 80.8%, Neospectra 85.0%, ICRAF 87.8%, Mango 88.9%. KSSL and ICRAF provide 65.8% of the forecasts. The unweighted mean over sources is 68.3%; for RPM-w it is 69.4% (CGL 56.7%, Tablets 33.0%, Diesel 54.9%).
issues.corrective_action: Report coverage per source and per task, with equal weights per source as the primary summary. Calibrate the bands stratified by family, or with a source-level exchangeability argument. Rephrase the abstract and recommendation (iii) to say that nominal coverage holds for soil libraries but not for small, non-soil sets.

issues.title: Temporal and campaign structure is ignored in the main analysis; the only temporal test (mango) shows that the conclusions do not transfer
issues.description: All main-analysis pilots, pools and test sets are random draws across the whole collection history. For mango this is 5 seasons and 114 populations, and season 5 ('Val Ext 2', 320 fruit) is in the main task but absent from the shift experiment. KSSL spans 23 annual cohorts (2001–2023), AfSIS1 spans 58 sentinel sites in 19 countries, and ICRAF-ISRIC spans many countries. In real sample-size planning the pilot comes from the first campaign and later samples come from later ones. The mango shift experiment (Table 4) shows that the method ranking reverses under this design (i.i.d. reference: RPM 0.328 vs FLAT 0.160; new season: RPM 0.115 vs FLAT 0.250). The audit's 'temporal leakage' row ('fruit-level i.i.d. estimand (documented)') does not address soils at all.
issues.evidence: load_mango (datasets.py L145–159) uses fruit-level groups across all seasons. robustness.py L113–120 uses seasons 1–3 → 4 only, with n0 ∈ {50, 100} and 10 pilots. KSSL soilsite observation.date.begin ranges from 2001-01-01 to 2023-01-01 (23 cohorts, 201–7,919 layers each), and the cap and split ignore it.
issues.corrective_action: Add a time- or campaign-ordered evaluation for at least KSSL (pilot and pool from earlier cohorts, test from later ones) and a country- or site-held-out evaluation for AfSIS1 and ICRAF. Report mango per season, including season 5. State in the abstract that the accuracy figures apply to random sampling within a fixed collection.
issues.proposed_experiment: KSSL-MIR and KSSL-VisNIR (4 properties): pool = cohorts 2001–2015, test = 2016–2023 (site-disjoint), with the same pilots and methods. AfSIS1: leave-sentinel-site- or country-out test split. Mango: leave-one-season-out over all 5 seasons.

issues.title: Sensitivity analysis S0 leaves in the exploratory data: ICRAF-MIR contains exactly the same soils and reference values as ICRAF-VisNIR
issues.description: The exploratory runs that fixed r = 1 and path matching used ICRAF-VisNIR (EXPERIMENT_LOG 18:52–18:58). S0 removes only the four ICRAF-VisNIR tasks. All ICRAF-MIR layers are ICRAF-VisNIR layers with identical labels, so the label noise floors that the paper itself shows govern the learning-curve slope remain in the 'held-out' set. In addition, the audit's 'Design informed by evaluation data' row lists only the r = 1 choice. It omits that RPM-T, SLOPE-T, the gain metric and the conformal bands were all specified after the authors had inspected main-run results computed on the test sets (EXPERIMENT_LOG 19:41, 14:53, 14:55).
issues.evidence: Cached layer IDs: 4,153 of 4,153 ICRAF-MIR layers are present in ICRAF-VisNIR, and both use the same ICRAF_ISRIC soillab and soilsite files (datasets.py L48–49, L91–92). The S0 table header states that only the ICRAF-VisNIR tasks are excluded (Section 4.3; Table S15).
issues.corrective_action: Repeat S0 excluding all 8 ICRAF tasks. Extend the audit row to list every post-hoc method and metric, with the results that had been seen when each was defined.

issues.title: DATA_LEAKAGE_AUDIT.md has unverifiable or inaccurate entries, and its 'verified by' column cannot detect real-data grouping errors
issues.description: Several audit statements cannot be reproduced from the shipped code, or are wrong. (a) The mango validation numbers ('0.006 vs 0.889') are produced by no script in the repository, and the distance metric is undefined. (b) 'AfSIS: repeated scans' are said to be averaged, but OSSL v1.3 AfSIS1 MIR has one row per layer. (c) 'Mango restricted to the standard-temperature scans' suggests that the temperature fruit keep their standard scan. In fact the 816 temperature-experiment lots have no standard-temperature rows and are dropped entirely. (d) 'Code review (Reviewer-4 round)' is not evidence a reader can check. (e) 'Unlabelled spectra = pool spectra only (never test spectra)' does not hold for the RPM-Uextra ablation, whose extra library spectra include layers from test-set sites. (f) Group-disjointness is 'verified' only on synthetic labels, which is why issue 01 went undetected.
issues.evidence: grep of the repository finds '0.889' only in the audit text itself. My recomputation (SNV, RMS distance over 94 bands) gives a within-pair median of 0.0020 vs 0.263 between fruits, the same conclusion with different numbers. AFSIS1/ossl_mir_v1.3.csv.gz has 18,250 rows and 18,250 unique id.layer_local_c. In the mango file, Temp != 'No' covers 816 lots and none of their (Season, Pop, Date, Cultivar, Type, DM) keys occurs among the 'No' rows. For RPM-Uextra (forecast_experiment.py L120–124), 1.4% (KSSL-MIR:OC), 2.0% (KSSL-MIR:clay) and 3.3% (KSSL-VisNIR:clay) of the extra unlabelled spectra come from test-set sites. The effect is negligible, but the statement is untrue. The KSSL claim (5,111 duplicates) checks out.
issues.corrective_action: Add a script (e.g., scripts/audit_checks.py) that regenerates every number in the audit from raw files. Add real-data tests that assert no shared profile, site or KSSL ID across pool and test sets, and no test-site spectra in any unlabelled set. Correct statements (b), (c) and (e), and replace (d) with concrete code references.

issues.title: Data licensing, terms of use and version provenance are incompletely documented
issues.description: LUCAS and the Serbian OSSL subset are excluded 'because of restrictive licences', yet the three Eigenvector data sets are used with 'no licence stated' (datasets.py meta), and the Data Availability statement simply says 'All data are public'. Tecator's permission note asks users to name the instrument and company (Tecator Infratec) in publications and to attach the note on redistribution; the manuscript text does not name the instrument. AfSIS1 is ODbL (share-alike), which matters if derived per-sample data are deposited. No SHA256SUMS.txt exists in data_raw even though code/README.md says one is written. The mango reference cites Mendeley version 6 (…46htwnp833.6), while the file used is 'MangoDMC_NIR_Data_v3.csv', downloaded via an unversioned file URL, and the OSSL bucket is mutable.
issues.evidence: datasets.py L140, L157, L209, L228, L271, L255; data_raw/tecator/tecator.arff header lines 10–19; ls data_raw (no SHA256SUMS.txt); manuscript reference [32]; scripts/download_data.py L24–25.
issues.corrective_action: Add a per-data-set table of licence or terms of use, version or DOI, download date and SHA-256. State the Eigenvector terms explicitly. Name the Tecator Infratec instrument. Pin the dataset versions.

issues.title: The 'irreducible-noise fraction' descriptor is normalised by the test-set variance
issues.description: alignment_table() computes noise_frac_full_pool = exp(log_sigma2) / var_test, where var_test is the variance of y on the held-out test set (refinement.py L40; forecast_experiment.py L50). This descriptor drives Fig. 4, the slope regression (R² = 0.73, Table S4) and the error correlates (Table S29). It does not affect forecasts, but a pool-only analysis should not use test labels, and the group-disjoint test sets of 58–164 samples make var_test noisy for the small sets.
issues.corrective_action: Normalise by the pool variance (or by the variance of the large-sample fit's own y), and recompute Fig. 4, Table S4 and Table S29.

issues.title: For soils, calibration and pilot samples are drawn as individual layers, whereas real campaigns sample whole profiles or sites
issues.description: Pilots (forecast_experiment.py L75) and truth subsets (learning_curves.py L62) are drawn row-wise, so an 'n-sample calibration' is n layers spread over up to n profiles. Real soil calibration campaigns collect and pay for whole profiles or sites. That yields fewer independent units per n, so learning curves are likely flatter and pilot LOGO errors higher than in this simulation. The resulting forecasts answer a less practical planning question than the paper suggests.
issues.evidence: rng.choice(pool, n0, replace=False) and rng.choice(pool, n, replace=False) operate on sample indices, not groups. ICRAF profiles have a median of 5 layers, and KSSL sites have several layers each (64,940 layers in 13,467 sites).
issues.corrective_action: Either state the estimand explicitly (layers drawn independently), or add a group-wise sampling variant for the soil tasks (pilots and truth subsets composed of whole sites) and report whether the conclusions change.
issues.proposed_experiment: For KSSL-MIR and ICRAF-MIR (4 properties each), redraw pilots and truth subsets as whole sites or profiles up to n layers, and compare the forecast errors of RPM, FLAT, SLOPE-T and IPL3 with the layer-wise results.

recommendation_rationale: The core finding, that power-law extrapolation from small pilots is optimistic and RPM beats IPL3, holds up at the source level (9 of 9 sources; p = 0.0039). Replicate averaging and pool-only unlabelled data are handled correctly. However, the manuscript claims leakage-free, group-disjoint evaluation, and that claim is false for 12 of 38 tasks (issue 01). The LOSO transfer treats a subset of KSSL as an independent source, and correcting this removes SLOPE-T's reported significant advantage (issue 02). Task-level inference ignores heavy sample sharing between tasks (issue 03). The ground truth for the small sets is dominated by a few samples from a single split (issue 04). The nominal-coverage claim for calibrated bands holds only for soils (issue 05). All of these can be fixed with corrected groups, provenance-based source definitions, hierarchical statistics and repeated outer splits. Several practical recommendations and abstract statements will likely need to be softened as a result.
